A welcome from Nnemoma

Welcome, healer! This playbook is for healers of every modality: breathwork guides, Reiki practitioners, sound healing practitioners, yoga teachers, etc., who want to be booked consistently in their own community.

You come from a long line of healers, many of whom had to hide their gifts. You are the one being called to be bold with yours. You are ancestrally guided to do this work, you are powerful, and it's time to show up like it.

Here's why this matters. Your community is full of people who need what you carry, and most of them don't know you offer it yet. When you're booked consistently close to home, you get steady income, clients you can see again and again, and a reputation that grows by word of mouth. That's how you become the go-to healer in your community, and the work starts coming to you.

Over the next 7 days, you'll learn how to invite the people already around you into your work, and you'll send your first 10 invitations.

This is not some boring ebook that you'll read once and never use again. You will end this journey by putting on your CEO cap and taking REAL action. Because if you wanted more of the same, you wouldn't be here, right? Let's get into it!

Who am I?

I'm Nnemoma, an African-centered breathwork guide and life coach. After a layoff from my tech career, I followed an intuitive nudge into breathwork training. I started leading sessions the way I was taught, trying to sound like every other guide online. My sessions were impactful but not memorable.

Everything shifted when I started leading with my actual medicine, African-centered breathwork with drums, African music, and movement, because that is how I am ancestrally led. And when I stopped waiting to be found and started inviting people directly into my work, my name and my medicine started to spread. Today I'm the go-to healer in my own community, leading recurring sessions with friends, family, neighbors, local businesses, schools and retreats. I've led 100+ sessions in the past 3 years, and learning to invite people directly was the skill that changed everything.

This playbook is how I do it, so you can too.

Section 3 of 9

Why outreach feels scary (and why it's time anyway)

Let's say it like it is. Reaching out to people about your work can feel scary. You don't want to sound salesy. You don't want to be cringey. You don't want to annoy people or feel like you're bothering someone who never asked to hear from you. So you wait. You post a little more, tweak your bio again, and hope your next clients find you. That fear makes sense.

But...while you're avoiding outreach because of the cringe factor, the people you've been assigned to serve, spiritually, are sitting in waiting for you. Some of them are stretched thin, weighed down by stress, and looking for exactly the medicine you serve. And some of them are booking another healer right now, only because that healer was bolder about their offerings.

So babes it's time to step into your CEO energy. You didn't receive your sacred gifts to continue keeping it quiet. The Divine entrusted you to birth this business, and being a good steward of it means getting it in front of the people it's meant for.

Outreach feels awkward when you don't have the words, the plan, or the tools. Once you have real tools at your fingertips, it stops feeling like selling and starts feeling like it's rooted in service as it's meant to be. That's what's in this playbook.

Is this you?
  • "I don't want to sound salesy." You won't. An invitation shares something of value and makes it easy to say yes or no.
  • "I don't want to annoy anyone." A clear, kind invitation with an easy out is not annoying, and one follow-up is not pestering.
  • "I don't know what to say." You will. This playbook gives you the words, a plan, and a template for every invitation.
Section 4 of 9

Intentional Invitations is a skill anyone can learn

Being good at outreach isn't a personality trait. It's a skill, and like any skill it gets easier with practice.

The first few invitations will feel like a stretch. That's the point. By invitation ten it feels different, and by invitation twenty it starts to feel normal. Every invitation is a rep, and every yes or no is proof. That proof builds real confidence, so you can talk about what you do clearly and hold your rate later.

Here's what else happens. The more you invite, the more you learn about the people you serve. You hear what stress they're carrying, which words land, and what they're really looking for. That makes every session, every offer, and every next invitation more aligned.

If you do not currently have a consistent practice of inviting people into your world right now, this will feel big. This is a mindset shift into that CEO energy, but you get to make it one small invitation at a time.

See an example below of a real invitation I sent, and how it landed.

Section 5 of 9

Deciding Who to Invite

Invitations, not pitches

A pitch pushes. An invitation opens a door. You're not convincing anyone. You're letting the people you're meant to serve know you exist, and people can't say yes to what they don't know about. (And with social media algorithms, you surely can't assume people are seeing all your content). So we need to meet Spirit halfway: do your part, and let Spirit handle the rest.

Get clear on your who

For your 1:1 invitations, picture the person you feel most called to serve. What stresses are they carrying, and what about your offer might feel like relief? For small businesses, think about the owner and their team. Who runs it, and what pressure do their people carry? When you can speak to them like real people, the invitation feels natural and the yes comes easier.

Start with who you already know

Most healers skip the people already around them and assume everyone knows what they do. They don't. Make a direct ask.

  • For 1:1 invitations: invite a friend who's been stretched thin, a neighbor, a coworker, a cousin who's been asking about your work. Tell them what you do and invite them to a 1:1 or upcoming group sessions.
  • For small businesses: the places you already visit, like the yoga or pilates studio where you take class, your gym, or the spa or wellness center you go to. Know someone who works there or owns a business? Ask for an introduction ("Do you think the owner would be open to a short session for the team?").

A warm introduction beats a cold message every time.

Types of places you can invite

  • Small businesses: gyms and fitness studios, day spas, dance studios, and holistic health shops
  • Wellness spaces: yoga and pilates studios, massage and acupuncture practices, chiropractic offices, wellness centers
  • Schools and campuses: schools, after-school programs, college wellness centers
  • Senior living: senior homes and assisted living
  • Community and faith: churches and faith groups, community centers, libraries, nonprofits
  • Workplaces: local offices, co-working spaces, companies
  • Housing: apartment communities
  • Hotels and retreat spaces: boutique hotels, retreat centers
  • Care and support organizations: women's shelters, resource centers, mental health practices and groups (offer sessions as wellness support, not treatment)
  • People you know: friends, family, neighbors, coworkers

Make your list of 10

Time to take some CEO action. Sit quietly, take a few deep breaths, and ask: who might benefit from my healing services? Write down who comes to mind. Then fill in your list:

  • 5 for 1:1 invitations: name, why you thought of them, and how you'll reach them (text, DM, or in person)
  • 5 for local small businesses: business name, the owner or contact, why they're aligned, and how you'll reach them. Make sure they share your values and invest in their people or customers.
    • Make the fifth one your stretch invitation, the one that feels a little too big.

You'll work from this list during your Invitation Week.

Section 6 of 9

Making the Invitation

The invitation formula

Five parts and one ask: a warm opening that says why you're reaching out to them in particular, who you are in one line, the invitation itself (what, who it's for, how long), an easy yes, and an easy out. (Don't worry, the template is in the next section).

Freedom blocks

For all work related to your business, but especially the most stressful like outreach, I recommend carving out a sacred freedom block (at least once a week). Start with a few minutes of breathwork and movement. Light a candle, play some good music, and call in your aligned clients. Then send out your invites. When you ground yourself first, you open up the divine field, so you can invite from a place of ease instead of pressure. (We're not healers with these magical powers for no reason right?? Might as well actively use it in our business too!)

Tracking and follow-ups

Keep a simple invitation log, in a notes app or a spreadsheet. For each invitation, note the name, the date you sent it, how you sent it, whether they replied, notes, and when you'll follow up. Most people say yes after a gentle follow-up. And remember, every no is redirection, not rejection. Follow up once, three to five days later, using the follow-up templates on Day 5 and Day 6 of your Invitation Week.

The numbers

Realistically it takes about 20 invitations to land 5 or more bookings. Ten invitations is your first round, so don't quit after a few no's. Sending 10 invitations is 10 opportunities for someone to say yes to you. That is 10 more than you're doing right now.

Ways to invite

This week you'll use warm introductions and direct messages. When your week is done, choose your top 2 or 3 from this list to expand the ways you invite people into your world:

  • Warm introductions through people you know
  • A free online session for friends and family, with a clear invitation at the end for 1:1 sessions
  • Passing out flyers in the neighborhood
  • A free or low-cost group event, with an offer at the end
  • Free sessions for aligned groups that lead to invitations for paid sessions
  • A direct email or DM to local orgs, hotels, and studios
  • Scouting Threads and social media for people looking for a practitioner
    • they may not be looking for exactly what you offer but it doesn't hurt to shoot your shot
  • A referral network with therapists and other practitioners
  • In-person networking: carry business cards
  • Say yes to invitations you receive to share your work (you never know what doors may open)
  • Reaching out to people and orgs you've worked with before and propose recurring sessions
